newsitem.title: UK: M&S turns up heat with UK home shopping move.
newsitem.headline: M&S turns up heat with UK home shopping move.

text.p: A move by Britain's top clothing retailer Marks & Spencer Plc into mail order looks set to raise the profile of home shopping in Britain and put more pressure on established players in the declining agency market, analysts said on Thursday.
M&S has joined a growing list of clothing retailers, including Next Plc and Burton Group Plc which have branched out into fast-growing direct mail order to expand their brand and boost sales.

Analysts see M&S's decision to introduce a clothing catalogue by next spring turning up the heat on current market leaders, especially Great Universal Stores Plc , which rely on agents for their sales.
"It's another nail in the coffin of unbranded agency mail order," said one retail analyst, who asked not to be identified.
Stiffer competition has already spurred some consolidation, with Sears Plc trying to sell its Freemans mail order to number two player Littlewoods for about 395 million pounds ($651 million).
Both businesses use agents who receive commission or free merchandise for getting sales.

Agency catalogues, typically the size of a telephone directory and selling everything from clothes to furniture, still account for 60 percent of the market. They developed in the days when credit was scarce but have declined in part now this is more freely available.

But agency mail order can still be highly profitable as GUS's track record showed until recently. But analysts say the future is in direct mail -- used by highly successful Next and now Marks & Spencer -- because it is more focused and linked to more aspirational brands.

Market leader GUS, with 25 percent of the market, is almost entirely an agency business, relying on 3.7 million agents to bring in orders. It has only a small direct mail catalogue business, Marshall Ward.
It too is being forced to look at selling direct. Chairman Lord Wolfson of Sunningdale has said the group is looking into expanding direct mail, using its agency mail order infrastructure.

Littlewoods has launched Index Extra as a direct mail alternative to its agency catalogues and Empire Stores, owned by French retail conglomerate Pinault Printemps La Redoute , has done the same via its parent company catalogue.

The growing popularity of smaller, specialised catalogues has prompted suggestions that Britain could see a U.S.-style mail order explosion. U.S. home-shopping firm Land's End, for example, has already been operating in Britain for several years.
But analysts said parallels with the U.S. market were misleading as a more highly concentrated population reduced the need for mail order and shopping was still a popular pastime.
"There are interesting opportunities in home shopping, but we believe most people still like going out shopping," said Richard Hyman of Verdict Research.
Verdict estimated Britain's 7.5 billion pound mail order market has seen its share of total retail sales fall to 3.74 percent from 4.61 percent a decade ago.
"We think it will gain share and the trend will be reversed, but it will be modest," Hyman said.
Analysts think Marks & Spencer stands a good chance of success, given its proven skills in retail systems and operational management.

Customers without access to the full M&S range will be able to buy it via the catalogue. It is seen as a way of squeezing more sales out of the British market without actually building new stores, they said.
Next's experience suggests direct mail can boost sales volumes considerably. Its Directory catalogue accounts for one third of the retail chain's sales, said another retail analyst.
Mail order also gives retailers valuable information about who is buying what, allowing them to predict demand.

"We're in an information war at the moment in retailing, with shops wanting to get to know as much about the customer as they can," said William Cullem, European retail analyst at Paribas. ($ = 0.606 British Pounds)
